children: Dual-train centrifugal air blower (Blowers A and B), driven by a 3-phase induction motor. One train operates at a time; the other is on standby. The active train is detected automatically from motor current.

For each timestamp on the active train: shaft power from electrical input, pressure ratio and dP across the machine, three efficiency methods (polytropic per ASME PTC 10 §5.4a, isentropic per §5.4, and fluid-power as a hydraulic indicator), max vibration across probes, and max bearing temperature across probes. Tiered alerts roll up to a single status (OK / Advisory / Alarm / Trip) per the open Manual.

Reference-grade proof of concept. Not a control system, not an SIS, not a substitute for a formal ASME PTC 10 acceptance test. Efficiency values are not clamped to 0-100 % - a value outside that range is a data-quality signal worth investigating.
Open the Manual button on the Dashboard tab for the full data contract, equation derivations, and operating envelope.

This dashboard monitors performance and mechanical health of a dual-train centrifugal air blower (Blowers A / B, one active at a time) driven by a 3-phase induction motor. It computes shaft power, pressure ratio and dP, three efficiency metrics, max vibration, max bearing temperature, and a tiered alert roll-up. Inputs are timestamped historian rows; outputs are KPI tiles, trend charts, an alert log, and an exportable CSV.

Scope is reference-grade PoC. The dashboard is not a control system, not an SIS, and not a substitute for a formal ASME PTC 10 acceptance test. Fluid-power efficiency is an incompressible-flow hydraulic indicator only and is not a thermodynamically rigorous compressor efficiency.

Centrifugal blower trains, single-stage, motor-driven through a direct or speed-increased coupling. Service is combustion air or process air at near-atmospheric suction. Suction is referenced as absolute (kPaa) because the suction-side instrumentation reads true absolute below atmospheric when the inlet filter is loaded. Discharge is referenced as gauge (kPag) because the discharge transmitter is plant-standard PI-tagged.

Vibration is monitored on up to 4 probes per train (typically two casing or bearing-housing points and two on the shaft or coupling area). Bearing temperature is monitored on up to 2 RTDs per train (drive end and non-drive end). Filter dP is monitored on the suction air filter to flag clogging. Bypass valve position is monitored to detect recycle and capacity-limit conditions.

Status is rolled up from independent checks and reported as a single overall pill on the banner: OK / Advisory / Alarm / Trip. Triple-encoded (color, dot, text) per ISA-101.

Advisory at Zone B/C boundary (default 4.5 mm/s). Alarm at C/D (7.1 mm/s). Trip at Zone D (11.0 mm/s, long-term operation not permissible). For flexible-foundation Group 1 or smaller-machine groups, retune the thresholds.

Filter dP greater than 0.10 bar (replace filter). Blower dP above design max (default 1.00 bar at the dashboard, originally 0.45 bar in engine.py - tune to nameplate). Bypass valve greater than 60 % open (recirculating excess flow). Bypass closed below 5 % combined with discharge pressure below setpoint (machine at capacity limit).

Suction is absolute (kPaa) because the suction-side transmitter is a true absolute reference and reads partial vacuum when the inlet air filter is loaded. Discharge is gauge (kPag) because the discharge transmitter is plant-standard PI-tagged. Internally the engine normalizes both to absolute bar before computing dP, ratio, and the thermodynamic efficiencies. Site atmospheric pressure is a configurable setting (default 0.93 bar for an inland Alberta site at roughly 700 m elevation). For coastal or high-altitude sites, set the atmospheric pressure to match.

All four trend charts share conventions. Solid line is the online value at each timestamp. Dashed line is a reference level (vibration advisory, bearing advisory, design dP). The right axis is reserved for the secondary metric in dual-axis charts (flow on the power chart, blower dP on the bearing chart). Series colors come from the Ferriq palette:

Gas is assumed to be air (

). Do not reuse this engine for process gases without updating the gamma setting. The motor power factor uses nameplate value (0.85); replace with measured PF if a recent test exists. Flow measurement is assumed accurate per ISO 5167 (orifice or venturi, typical ±2 % full scale); no uncertainty propagation in this PoC.

Suction temperature is forward-filled up to 4 hours when missing, then falls back to a fixed default of 4.0 °C. Discharge temperature is required for the thermodynamic efficiencies. If only one train has a discharge transmitter, the dashboard reports n_isentropic and n_polytropic as blank when the un-instrumented train is active and falls back to fluid-power as the headline. Vibration interpretation uses ISO 10816-3 Group 1; for flexible-foundation or smaller machines, retune the thresholds via the limits inputs.

Steady, monotonic climb in max bearing T over weeks while load is constant. Suggests lube-oil contamination, cooling-water side fouling, or seal wear. Demo data shows this signature - bearing T2 climbs from 54 °C (Dec 16) to 75 °C (Jan 28), crossing the 70 °C advisory mid-January.
Step or ramp increase in max vibration across one or more probes with no change in current or pressure. Suggests rotor unbalance, coupling wear, or impeller fouling.
Filter dP climbs above 0.10 bar at constant flow. Suction pressure drops below the typical envelope. Replace filter.
Bypass position pinned greater than 60 % at non-startup conditions. Recycling flow, increasing energy cost. Investigate controller setpoint and bypass actuator.
Bypass closed below 5 % and discharge pressure below setpoint. Machine cannot meet demand at current speed. Consider second train start or downstream demand reduction.

ASME PTC 10 - Performance Test Code on Compressors and Exhausters (isentropic and polytropic efficiency definitions, §5.4, §5.4a). API 617 - Axial and Centrifugal Compressors and Expander-Compressors (polytropic as primary). ISO 10816-3 - Mechanical vibration evaluation of machines, in-situ measurements (Group 1 zone boundaries B/C, C/D, D). ISO 5167 - Measurement of fluid flow by means of pressure differential devices (orifice plates, nozzles, venturi tubes). ASHRAE Handbook - Fundamentals (air properties, gamma value).

Every price on this dashboard is either published by a government agency or calculated from prices that are. Nothing is a private assessment and nothing is bought. The table below names each publisher and says how current its figures are.
the formula behind every number in the price panel

Products fall into four groups. Two have a real traded benchmark. Two are anchored on an Alberta price and moved daily. Three have no external price at all, because their value depends on where the refinery sends them.
the full arithmetic, checkable by hand

These two products are priced in two stages. The Government of Alberta publishes a reference price each month, in Canadian dollars per cubic metre, which sets the level. That figure lags about two months, so it is rolled forward to today using a daily US benchmark: the Alberta price is scaled by how far that benchmark has moved since the Alberta month's own average.

No exchange rate appears anywhere in this calculation. The Alberta price is already Canadian, and the daily benchmark enters as a ratio of two US prices, which cancels out. Applying a rate to either would count it twice.
How the Crude Feed Is Priced
two stages, kept separate on purpose
feed price = WCS + that feed's grade differential

Alberta publishes the differential monthly and as a positive discount; the model takes it as negative, since WCS trades below WTI. WTI itself is a daily price, so the pair together give a daily WCS estimate rather than a month-old one. The exchange rate is applied once, at the very end, and never inside the differential arithmetic.

Grade differentials are a calibration snapshot rather than market assessments. One feed matches a named published stream exactly; the rest are proxies. The Data & Log tab shows which is which for each feed.

The margin on the Dashboard tab is calculated from the fixed low and high prices in the Data & Log tab, not from the live estimates. The table below compares the two. Where they disagree, both are shown as they are: no factor is fitted, scaled, or calibrated to bring a market estimate into line with an assumed price. A disagreement is a result worth looking at, not an error to remove.

The coker correlations take the feed's Conradson carbon residue and return gas, naphtha, coke and gas oil, which sum to 100 wt% by construction. This model then divides the gas oil between diesel, LVGO, MVGO and HVGO using this plant's own proportions rather than the generic split in the literature, because those cut points belong to the fractionator and do not change when the upstream reactor does.
Why catalytic cracking sits on the gas oil, not the vacuum residue.

An FCC runs on gas oil. The unconverted oil leaving the SimDist split in this model is 99.7% vacuum gas oil, so that stream, not the vacuum residue, is where the unit belongs. Hydrocracking and catalytic cracking are the two established competing routes for converting gas oil, which is what makes them a genuine either-or: hydrocracking adds hydrogen and favours kerosene and diesel, catalytic cracking rejects carbon and favours gasoline-range material and LPG.

All data used in this model were obtained from open, publicly available sources. No proprietary, licensed or purchased data is used anywhere in it.

Prices come from Government of Alberta open data and the U.S. Energy Information Administration, both free public services. Process yields come from the source costing spreadsheet and from published refining literature. Crude quality data come from public crude assay information.
Every figure this model produces is an estimate rather than a market assessment, and none of it should be used to settle a transaction.
These are bulk values at the refinery gate.
No pump prices, no consumer fuel tax, no retail margin. The model represents the economics of the refinery, not of the fuel retail chain.
The US benchmarks are Gulf Coast prices.

This refinery is in Western Canada, so a real basis difference exists between the two markets. No basis adjustment is applied, because there is no defensible figure to apply. The two Alberta-anchored products avoid this, since their anchor is already an Alberta price.
Butane has no daily published price.
Its Alberta anchor is real, but the daily movement borrows the gasoline benchmark. That is the weakest link in the product pricing and it affects LPG.
Pentanes plus is condensate, not a refinery naphtha cut.
It remains a proxy for naphtha, though a much closer one than finished gasoline, which is a blended consumer fuel and trades well above a blendstock.
Unconverted oil has no live price at all.

The US stopped publishing residual fuel oil prices in 2022, so it is valued as a fraction of the heavy crude price. That fraction is the first thing to revisit if a heavy-product assessment becomes available.

Crude to Profit prices a five-crude refinery blend from feedstock to finished product. Five Canadian crude streams blend into one feed, split on a per-crude assay yield into primary distillation cuts, and the two heavy cuts convert further: vacuum residue through a residue hydrocracker, and the leftover unconverted oil through a hydrocracker/hydrotreater. The resulting seven-product slate is priced against the crude feed cost at a low and a high price case, in C$/hr and million C$/yr.

This is a margin screening tool. It does not optimize the blend, respect unit capacity limits, or check that a product meets specification. It answers what this blend earns at these prices for a fixed configuration, not what blend to buy.

Six stages run in order. Crude blend combines the five feeds and reports each crude's share, sulfur load, and flow in barrels. Primary distillation applies each crude's assay yield table to split it into naphtha, AGO, VGO, vacuum residue, and the three VGO sub-cuts (LVGO, MVGO, HVGO). Residue Hydrocracker converts the vacuum residue into naphtha, a diesel cut, three VGO grades, and an unconverted bottoms stream, on a mass balance basis at a fixed feed and product density. Each intermediate stream then splits into the seven finished cuts on its own per-stream split table. The unconverted oil left over from that split becomes the hydrocracker/hydrotreater feed and splits again on its own yield table, where LPG is the C3 plus iC4 plus nC4 roll-up. Economics sums crude cost and product revenue at a low and a high price case and reports the difference as gross margin, annualised at 24 hours a day and 330 operating days a year.
Cut point: a diagnostic, not a driver

The dashboard reports a cut point of 367°C as a fixed, read-only figure. In the source model this number only feeds a display column. It does not change the product slate; the finished-product volumes come entirely from the per-stream split tables in the Data & Log tab. Treat the cut point as a reference for how well the split assumption matches a real distillation curve, not as a control that shifts output.

This model routes the naphtha stream differently from the spreadsheet it was built from, which lifts the margin by roughly 39 %. The volume balance closes exactly here: everything fed into the product split comes back out. Worth walking through together before the figures are used.

Crude and product prices come from two public sources, and the panel on the Dashboard tab shows the publication date of every figure it uses. The Government of Alberta publishes Western Canadian Select, WTI, and the spread between them. The U.S. Energy Information Administration publishes daily spot prices for crude and refined products. The exchange rate is fetched daily.

Crude is priced in two steps. A daily WCS is estimated first, from WTI and the published WCS-WTI spread, because the spread moves slowly while the outright price tracks WTI day to day. Each feed is then priced as WCS plus a differential for its grade, and the result converts to Canadian dollars per cubic metre once, at the end. The crude table lists the grade each feed is priced against.

Products are valued four ways. Kerosene and diesel have real traded benchmarks, against Gulf Coast jet fuel and ULSD. LPG and naphtha are anchored on the Government of Alberta’s monthly NGL reference prices, which are Alberta prices already quoted in Canadian dollars per cubic metre, and rolled forward to today by a daily US benchmark. The two swing cuts and unconverted oil have no external price at all and are calculated instead. The Sources & Formulas tab shows the arithmetic for each.

A swing cut is worth whatever pool it is sent to, so its value is derived rather than looked up. The 128 to 145 C cut is valued between the naphtha and kerosene pools, and the 340 to 385 C cut between unconverted oil and the diesel pool. The split between destinations is a model setting. Unconverted oil is valued as a fraction of the heavy crude price, because no live heavy-product benchmark is published any more.

Every figure is a bulk value at the refinery gate. None of it includes consumer fuel tax, retail markup, or station margin, and no pump prices are used anywhere. The model represents the economics of the refinery, not of the fuel-retail chain. The benchmarks are US market prices while the refinery is in Western Canada, so a real basis difference remains and is deliberately left at zero rather than guessed at.

All of these are estimates drawn from benchmarks, not assessed prices for these specific streams. The model runs on the fixed reference prices in the Data and Log tab unless live prices are applied deliberately, so the headline margin does not move on its own.

This engine prices one blend at one set of yields. It is volumetrically additive with no shrinkage correction on blending, and the Residue Hydrocracker step converts every product on a single generic density (862 kg/m³) rather than a per-product one, matching the source workbook's own simplification. Utilities, hydrogen, catalyst, labour, and capital charges sit outside the boundary; the reported figure is a gross crude-to-product margin, not a net cash margin. The 330 operating days a year is an availability assumption, not a measurement. Crude density and sulfur are fixed reference values from assay data, not live feeds.

The bundled demo dataset covers 60 daily aggregated rows interpolated backwards from a single client-supplied operating snapshot, with realistic per-channel noise applied. This is a daily-aggregated dashboard. The 1H and 24H pills resolve correctly but show the latest day on a finer grid; full sub-daily resolution requires a historian connection.
Stack temperature creep over weeks, efficiency falling:
convection-bundle fouling. Schedule offline cleaning. Verify with bridgewall temp (should also rise slightly as heat shifts from convection back to radiant).
drifting up, excess air rising, efficiency falling:
burner air-register drift or damper opening creep. Check air register positions and FD damper modulation.
dropping below 2 %, CO sensor (if present) ramping:
incomplete combustion. Trim air register up immediately. Risk of soot deposition and tube fire-side fouling.
Bridgewall climbing while stack temp normal:
radiant-section tube fouling on the process side. Check process pressure drop and tube skin temperatures.
Heat-balance and PTC 4 efficiency agree but process-side disagrees:
process flow meter or Cp_p error. Audit the meter calibration and confirm fluid composition.
Heat-balance and process-side agree but PTC 4 disagrees:
ambient-temperature sensor drift, or radiation-loss assumption out of date for the heater. Recalibrate or update the loss percentage.

Each test point is a 24-hour-ahead forecast from a chronologically prior state. P10 and P90 are the data-driven 80% prediction interval. Empirical coverage = % of actuals that fall inside the band; target is 80%. Lower coverage means the model is under-confident (real-world readings lie outside the predicted band more often than expected).

Forecasts when any radiant tube skin thermocouple in a fired heater pass will reach 475 °C, the polythionic stress corrosion cracking limit for 9Cr-1Mo and 5Cr-0.5Mo tube alloys per API 530. Operating above 475 °C requires soda ash neutralization wash on shutdown. The forecast lets operators plan throughput cuts or decoke timing before the limit is hit.

The Hold-out validation card above lets you verify model accuracy on data it never trained on. Empirical coverage of the P10-P90 band is reported per TC; values below 80% indicate the model is under-confident on that TC and the actual readings lie outside the band more often than the model predicts.

The trained 24-hour-ahead predictor is rolled forward in 24-hour steps for 7 days. The dashboard linearly interpolates the resulting trajectory to find the time at which it crosses 475 °C. If no crossing is found within 7 days, the slope between current and day-7 prediction is extrapolated.

Each thermocouple has THREE trained XGBoost models per TC: P10 (10th percentile), P50 (median, central forecast), and P90 (90th percentile). Trained with objective='reg:quantileerror' and quantile_alpha = 0.1 / 0.5 / 0.9. The chart band shown between P10 and P90 is the data-driven 80% prediction interval. All three models walk forward recursively and the band evolves naturally as the forecast horizon extends.

The forecast tile headline checks both the central P50 trajectory AND the upper P90 band. If P50 doesn't cross 475 but P90 does within the 7-year internal horizon, the tile reports 'Possible in N days (upper bound)'. Empirical coverage of the P10-P90 band on hold-out data ranges from ~50 to ~95% across TCs (target 80%) - reported in the About tab.

The history chart now shows ONE pass at a time, with each individual radiant skin thermocouple on that pass drawn as its own line. Use the 'show pass' pill bar in the chart head to switch which pass is displayed. Solid lines = historical readings per TC. Dashed lines = per-TC P50 forecast (central). Filled bands = per-TC P10-P90 quantile-regression prediction interval (data-driven, 80% nominal coverage). Dashed red horizontal = 475 °C alarm. Dashed amber = 460 °C advisory. The four pass-level summary tiles at the top of the page remain unaffected by the chart selection - they always reflect every pass.

The topbar has TWO independent time controls. The PAST group (7D / 30D / 90D + custom 'd back' input) drives the history x-axis backward from the latest dataset timestamp; default is 30D. The FORECAST group (+7D / +90D / +1Y + custom 'd fwd' input) drives how far forward the chart shows the prediction trajectory; default is +7D. The forecast tile values (hours-to-475, 'Not expected within 7 years' verbiage, etc.) are computed once over a fixed 7-year internal horizon and do NOT change with the FORECAST pill. The pill only changes what slice of that trajectory the chart displays. For long horizons the chart x-axis is downsampled (weekly above 90D, biweekly above 1Y) to stay readable.

Pass 4 of Heater 2 has wider P10-P90 bands than other passes due to TC dropouts in the source data; treat its forecasts with extra skepticism. Heater 3 has only 3 thermocouples total across the heater, so per-pass forecasting is limited to one combined pass.

The predictor uses a hybrid forecast composition: a linear regression on the last 30 days of skin-TI history (slope in °C/day) provides the central trajectory at every forecast horizon, and three XGBoost quantile models per TC (P10, P50, P90) provide the data-driven uncertainty band. Linear extrapolation correctly extends fouling trends beyond the training-data range; the quantile band captures normal day-to-day variation around the trend. At each forecast step, the band width = P90-P50 (upper) and P50-P10 (lower) from the XGBoost quantile spread, decorating the linear central. Per-TC modelling lets the dashboard monitor every thermocouple individually. Training uses chronological 80/20 split: first 80 percent of dates train, most recent 20 percent are held-out test, which tests whether the band widths reflect real out-of-sample variation.

Turnaround and upset rows are detected and excluded from training. A turnaround row is one where the maximum skin TI across all TCs in the furnace falls below 250 °C (cold furnace), dilated by 3 days each side to capture cool-down approach and warm-up startup transients. An upset row is one where the day-over-day change in max skin TI exceeds 50 °C (sensor glitch or large process disturbance). Across the three furnaces, 6 to 13 percent of rows are excluded as turnaround/upset; the remaining stable-operation data trains a model that is not biased by shutdown trajectories.

Decoke detection: each turnaround group is compared against the 7 days before and after. If post-restart skin TI is at least 30 °C lower than pre-shutdown, the turnaround is classified as a decoke (tube cleaning happened, fouling clock resets) and a new run begins. Otherwise the shutdown is treated as a maintenance stop and the previous run continues. The engineered feature days_since_run_start counts only operating time within the current run, so different runs align at t=0 instead of being averaged together. This is critical for fouling-rate prediction: the model now sees N independent fouling curves instead of one smeared curve over 5 years. The dashboard about-tab shows decoke dates and current days-into-run per furnace.

Hyperparameters: max_depth = 3, n_estimators = 80, learning_rate = 0.06, subsample = 0.85, colsample_bytree = 0.85. Three quantile models per TC (P10, P50, P90) using objective='reg:quantileerror'. Trees are dumped to a compact JSON node format and evaluated by a pure-JavaScript walker in this dashboard.

Feature set per pass: pass flow, IP steam injection, convection skin TI, crossover T, pass outlet T, calculated pass duty (where available), whole-furnace radiant box T, fuel gas flow, combustion air, plus engineered features for current-skin-max, 7-day rolling mean, skin-velocity (degC/day), cumulative duty integral, and days-since-data-start (proxy for cumulative coke deposition).
Retraining cadence: as new operating data accumulates, re-run train.py against the updated Excel. The dashboard will pick up the new model.json bundle on next load.

The lab and online permeate analyzers measure on slightly different bases (mol % via gas chromatograph vs. vol % via thermal conductivity or NDIR). For ideal-gas refinery streams the difference is well below the noise floor, so the two are compared directly.

This dashboard does not include pressure-based limits in the standard build. If the source data carries shell-side or tube-side pressure-drop tags (kPa or bar), the engine accepts them via the optional

aliases for export, but they are not evaluated by the alert logic. Pressure-drop trending is appropriate when fouling is being diagnosed against a known clean baseline DP, which is out of scope for this single-equipment view.
All temperatures are in °C. Internally the LMTD calculation works in temperature differences so the °C / K choice cancels.

All measured series are continuous lines. Design, advisory, and alarm reference lines are dashed: design in neutral gray, advisory in amber (#C4890E), alarm in red (#D4432A). Chart series colors are restricted to the gold and supporting palette - red (#D4432A) is reserved for status semantics and never used as a normal data line.

The topbar pill bar (1H, 24H, 7D, 30D, 90D) and the inline custom range (number + unit) drive both the trend chart x-axis and the Performance Averages KPI row. The Current Values row is unaffected by the range and always reflects the latest reading in the dataset.

The chart x-axis is padded to the full requested window. If the dataset is shorter than the window, the older portion shows as blank space (the line drops to nothing) rather than being compressed onto a shorter axis.
Window cutoff is computed off the latest dataset timestamp, not off wall-clock time. Demo data and historical CSV uploads behave the same way.

Per-row Cp values are taken at face value from the input feed. In real service Cp is temperature-dependent; the demo data uses spot-evaluated Cp at each row's temperature, which is the cleanest assumption for a shell-and-tube tracking tool.

Mass flow values can carry ±2 - 5 % uncertainty depending on meter type (orifice vs Coriolis vs ultrasonic). The Q imbalance check at 8 % is set to absorb typical instrumentation noise without firing on every row.

The engine assumes single-phase fluids on both sides. Phase change (vaporization, condensation) violates the m·Cp·ΔT formulation and will produce wildly biased Q values. Reboiler and condenser duty tracking needs a different model.

The F-factor calc assumes N shell passes with 2N tube passes (TEMA E with longitudinal baffle). For TEMA G, H, J, X or other non-standard geometries the formula does not apply; F should be entered manually or U computed without the F correction.
